To compute ${f}^{′}(x),$ we first make the substitution $u=3x-5$ and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{3x-5}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

The limit $u$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of the definite integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(-{\int }_{1}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{1}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{1}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2u-1)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x-5)\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2u-1)) \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(3x-5)-1) \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x-11).\end{aligned}
$$
